description: Toy Story, iPhone filmmaking, Netflix and IMAX: how digital technology democratised cinema.
content_html:
Toy Story and the First Computer-Generated Feature: 1995

In 1995, Pixar Animation Studios released Toy Story, the world’s first feature-length film made entirely with computer-generated animation. Directed by John Lasseter and co-produced with Disney, the film ran for 77 minutes and was generated entirely by computers — no hand-drawn frames, no physical sets, no photographed actors. Every surface, shadow, and movement was calculated by software. The film was a commercial and critical success, and it announced a new era in animated filmmaking.

A critical distinction is worth fixing in memory here: Toy Story was not the first film to use computer-generated imagery. Live-action films had been incorporating CGI elements since the 1980s, and significant milestones — the Terminator 2 and Jurassic Park achievements of the early 1990s — preceded it. What made Toy Story historically significant was that it was the first feature-length film composed entirely of computer-generated images, with no photography involved in the image-making. This distinction matters: exam questions specifically ask about the “first computer-generated feature”, not the “first film with CGI”.

Key Fact

Toy Story (1995), directed by John Lasseter at Pixar Animation Studios (co-produced with Disney), was the world’s first feature-length computer-generated animated film. It was not the first film with CGI, but the first feature composed entirely of computer-generated images.

Digital Cinematography and the DV Revolution

Alongside the rise of computer animation, the 1990s and 2000s brought a revolution in how live-action films were captured. Film stock — celluloid — had been the standard recording medium since cinema’s earliest days. It was expensive to buy, expensive to process, and limited in quantity: a director had a finite number of takes before the cost became prohibitive. Digital cinematography changed this calculation fundamentally. Digital sensors recorded to memory cards or hard drives; footage could be reviewed immediately on set; takes were essentially free. This changed the economics and culture of production.

Consumer-grade digital video (DV) cameras also began to appear in the late 1990s: small, lightweight, affordable, and capable of producing images that could be broadcast or projected. The “DV revolution” made it possible for filmmakers without studio budgets or studio equipment to produce feature-length work. Directors such as Lars von Trier used consumer DV cameras deliberately, as an aesthetic and political statement about cinema’s relationship to expensive technology. The rough, video-like quality of DV footage — its specific colour response, its softness, its visible grain in low light — became a recognisable aesthetic in independent filmmaking of the late 1990s and 2000s.

Citizen Filmmaking: Tangerine and the Smartphone

By the 2010s, smartphone cameras had reached a quality that made serious filmmaking possible on a device that fits in a pocket. The landmark moment in mainstream cinema came in 2015 with Tangerine, directed by Sean Baker. The film was shot entirely on an iPhone 5S using the Filmic Pro app and anamorphic lenses attached to the phone. It premiered at the Sundance Film Festival and received wide critical acclaim, demonstrating that a compelling, professional-quality narrative feature could be made for a fraction of the cost of conventional film production.

Tangerine’s visual approach was partly a consequence of its shooting method. The iPhone’s wide-angle lens naturally produced a specific look: faces often filled much of the frame, backgrounds fell away into soft-focus colour, and the camera could move through the bustle of Los Angeles streets with an immediacy that a conventional film camera rig could not match. The film’s energy and intimacy were inseparable from the technology used to make it. This is a key principle: technology does not just determine what is possible; it shapes the aesthetic character of what is made.

The phrase “democratisation of production” refers to the way that digital and smartphone technology reduced the cost barrier to making films. In the era of celluloid, a feature-length film required expensive film stock, laboratory processing and specialist camera equipment — barriers that effectively restricted filmmaking to those with institutional backing. Digital cameras, editing software and smartphone devices removed most of those barriers. Anyone with a phone and a free editing app can now shoot and distribute a short film. The question this raises — relevant for Film Studies at any level — is what this means for whose stories get told and which voices get heard. Films like Tangerine told stories about communities (transgender sex workers in Los Angeles) that the Hollywood studio system had historically ignored, using equipment that the studio system would never have sanctioned.

Netflix and the Streaming Revolution

Netflix was founded in 1997 as a postal DVD rental service. In 2007, it launched its online streaming service, initially for a small catalogue of titles. Growth was rapid. By 2013 Netflix was producing its own original content; by 2016 it had over 80 million subscribers globally. The tipping point came in 2017 when streaming overtook DVD as the primary distribution method for film and television content in the United States. Physical media — the disc in the box on the shelf — had been the dominant home-viewing format since the 1980s; within a decade of Netflix’s streaming launch, it was secondary.

The implications for cinema were profound. Films could reach global audiences without a theatrical release; directors who might not have attracted studio backing found Netflix willing to fund adventurous projects. The traditional window between theatrical release and home viewing, which had been several months, compressed dramatically — and with the Covid-19 pandemic of 2020 closed cinemas worldwide, some major releases went directly to streaming. For audiences, streaming meant access to an enormous catalogue on demand, at home, without scheduling. For the film industry, it raised questions about what “cinema” means when most viewers watch films on a laptop or phone screen.

Key Fact

Netflix launched its streaming service in 2007. By 2017, streaming had overtaken DVD as the primary distribution format for film and television content in the United States, fundamentally changing how audiences accessed cinema.

IMAX and the Blockbuster Spectacle: Avengers: Infinity War (2018)

At the same time as smartphone cinema was making production cheaper and more accessible, the premium end of filmmaking was pushing in the opposite direction: towards the largest, highest-resolution cameras ever used in mainstream fiction production. The IMAX format had been used in documentary and nature films since the 1970s and in partial sequences of mainstream releases from the early 2000s. In 2018, Avengers: Infinity War, directed by Anthony and Joe Russo, became the first major fiction feature to be shot entirely on IMAX cameras. Every frame was captured at the maximum resolution available, producing an image quality that could fill a six-storey screen with detail visible to the last row of the auditorium. The film was designed to be a theatrical event — an argument that cinema in a premium auditorium offers an experience categorically different from anything available at home.

Many students write that a film was “shown in IMAX” and think this is the same as saying it was “shot on IMAX cameras”. These are completely different things. Most films shown in IMAX cinemas are standard productions digitally upscaled for the large screen — the IMAX branding refers to the presentation format, not the capture format. Avengers: Infinity War (2018) was historically significant because it was the first major fiction feature shot entirely using IMAX cameras during production. The difference in image quality between footage shot on IMAX cameras and footage upscaled for IMAX projection is substantial. Do not conflate the two in exam answers.
exam_tip_html: The most frequent error on this topic is confusing Toy Story (1995) — the first feature-length computer-generated film — with the first film to use CGI. CGI appeared in live-action films earlier in the 1990s; Toy Story was the first entirely computer-generated feature. Similarly, many students write “IMAX” when they mean “shot entirely on IMAX cameras” — these are different things, and the exam will test the distinction. For “explain the effect” questions, the key move is to state what the technology changed for filmmakers or audiences. The democratisation of production question invites you to say: cheaper digital technology made it possible for directors outside the studio system to tell stories that would otherwise not have been made. Give a specific example: Tangerine (2015), Sean Baker, iPhone 5S.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Toy Story (1995, Pixar/Disney, directed by John Lasseter) was the world’s first feature-length computer-generated animated film — not the first film with CGI, but the first feature made entirely without photography.
  • Digital and smartphone technology democratised film production: Tangerine (2015, Sean Baker) was shot on an iPhone 5S, demonstrating that low-cost tools could produce professional, acclaimed narrative cinema and tell stories the studio system ignored.
  • Netflix launched streaming in 2007; by 2017 it had overtaken DVD as the primary distribution format. Meanwhile, Avengers: Infinity War (2018) became the first major fiction feature shot entirely on IMAX cameras — the highest and lowest cost ends of the industry developing in parallel.

practice_questions.text: Which film, released in 1995, was the world's first feature-length computer-generated animated film?
What is meant by the term 'streaming' in relation to film distribution?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that streaming is a method of delivering film content over the internet directly to the viewer's device; 1 mark for explaining that it requires no physical media (such as DVD or Blu-ray) and no downloading of files — content is accessed and played in real time.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect that digital cinematography had on the economics of film production, and how this contributed to the democratisation of filmmaking.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that digital cinematography removed the per-take cost of film stock (no expensive celluloid to buy or process); 1 mark for explaining that footage could be reviewed immediately on set, encouraging more experimentation; 1 mark for identifying that consumer-grade digital and smartphone cameras made equipment affordable outside the studio system; 1 mark for linking this to the democratisation of production (filmmakers from communities previously excluded by cost barriers could now make feature films); 1 mark for a named example such as Tangerine (2015, Sean Baker, iPhone 5S) or for accurate use of terminology.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the development of smartphone filmmaking, as demonstrated by Tangerine (2015), changed what kinds of stories cinema could tell and whose stories were told.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The answer explains what Tangerine demonstrated technically (shot entirely on iPhone 5S with anamorphic lens adaptor; Filmic Pro app) and articulates how the technology shaped the aesthetic (close framing, immediacy, soft-focus backgrounds). The answer then makes the macro-level argument: the low cost and mobility of smartphone cameras enabled directors without studio budgets to make work about communities and stories that the traditional studio system's financial logic had excluded. Tangerine's subject matter (transgender sex workers in Los Angeles) is identified as an example of a story that found a form of production suited to its scale and community. The link between technology (micro: specific camera choice, specific visual properties) and institutional/representational consequence (macro: democratisation, diversification of whose stories are told) is explicit and sustained. Specialist vocabulary is precise throughout.
Secure: The technological facts are correct and the main point about democratisation is made. Some link between the specific camera and its aesthetic effect is present. Subject matter of Tangerine is referenced.
Developing: The film is correctly identified as shot on an iPhone but analysis of the aesthetic or representational consequence is thin. Vocabulary is present but imprecise.
Emerging: Basic correct identification of the film with little or no analysis of effect on storytelling or representation.

practice_questions.text: In what year did Netflix launch its online streaming service?
Explain why Avengers: Infinity War (2018) is historically significant in relation to IMAX technology, and what effect this had on the audience's cinema experience.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that Avengers: Infinity War (2018, directed by Anthony and Joe Russo) was the first major fiction feature shot entirely on IMAX cameras; 1 mark for distinguishing this from films merely shown in IMAX (upscaled presentation vs capture format); 1 mark for explaining that IMAX cameras produce images significantly larger and sharper than standard 35mm; 1 mark for explaining the effect on audience experience (the image quality could fill a six-storey screen with detail visible from the back, creating a theatrical spectacle qualitatively different from home viewing); 1 mark for relating this to the broader context (studios competing with streaming platforms by offering a premium theatrical experience that cannot be replicated at home).

flashcard_questions.q: What was Toy Story (1995) the first example of?
flashcard_questions.a: The first feature-length film made entirely from computer-generated images.

flashcard_questions.q: Who directed Toy Story (1995) and which studios made it?
flashcard_questions.a: John Lasseter; Pixar Animation Studios, co-produced with Disney.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key distinction between Toy Story and earlier films with CGI?
flashcard_questions.a: Toy Story was entirely computer-generated; earlier films merely incorporated CGI elements alongside live action.
Capturing images onto digital storage rather than photographic film, removing the per-foot cost of film stock.

flashcard_questions.q: Which film demonstrated that a feature could be made entirely on a smartphone?
flashcard_questions.a: Tangerine (2015), directed by Sean Baker, shot on an iPhone 5S.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the 'democratisation of production' mean?
flashcard_questions.a: Falling technology costs making filmmaking accessible to people previously excluded by high equipment costs.

flashcard_questions.q: In what year did Netflix launch its streaming service?
When did streaming overtake DVD as the main home-viewing format in the US?
What is streaming in film distribution?
flashcard_questions.a: Delivering film content over the internet to a viewer's device in real time, without physical media.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was Avengers: Infinity War (2018) historically significant for IMAX?
flashcard_questions.a: It was the first major fiction feature shot entirely on IMAX cameras during production.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between 'shown in IMAX' and 'shot on IMAX cameras'?
flashcard_questions.a: Shown in IMAX means upscaled presentation; shot on IMAX means the actual production cameras were IMAX-format.

flashcard_questions.q: What is computer-generated animation as a distinct category?
flashcard_questions.a: A film made entirely from computer-generated images, with no live-action photography involved.

glossary_terms.definition: A film made entirely from images generated by computer software, with no live-action photography; distinct from films that merely incorporate CGI elements alongside photographed footage.
A method of capturing moving images directly onto electronic storage as digital data rather than onto photographic film, removing the per-foot cost of film stock.
The process by which falling costs and widening access to production technology make filmmaking available to people and communities who were previously excluded by the high cost of equipment.
A method of delivering film and television content over the internet directly to the viewer's device, without downloading the file and without the need for physical media such as DVD or Blu-ray.
A large-format film and digital camera and projection system producing images significantly larger and sharper than standard 35mm film, used for a premium theatrical experience.
Light-sensitive plastic film coated with chemical emulsion, used as the recording medium for cinema from its earliest days until the digital era.
